original_authorities_read.small_original_excerpt: A Noul answer is a single probability p p p that the answer is yes, and TypeSafe returns no separate confidence for it. The probability already carries the uncertainty: a value near 0.5 is the model saying it is unsure. A good starting point is 0.7 for yes and 0.3 for no, and the Noul page covers when to move them. If you want a confidence-style number anyway, for example to gate Nouls and Choices with the same code, use the distance from 0.5: confidence = ∣ 2 p − 1 ∣ \text{confidence} = |2p - 1| confidence = ∣2 p − 1∣ This gives 0 at p = 0.5 p = 0.5 p = 0.5 and 1 at p = 0 p = 0 p = 0 or p = 1 p = 1 p = 1 . It is also the Choice formula below applied to a yes-or-no Choice, so it sits on the same scale as Choice confidence. ​ Choice A Choice extends the same idea to any number of options. For a Choice with n n n options, where p max ⁡ p_{\max} p m a x ​ is the probability of the selected option: confidence = p max ⁡ − 1 n 1 − 1 n \text{confidence} = \frac{p_{\max} - \frac{1}{n}}{1 - \frac{1}{n}} confidence = 1 − n 1 ​ p m a x ​ − n 1 ​ ​ This measures how far the top probability sits above an even split of 1 n \frac{1}{n} n 1 ​ per option, on a scale where the even split is 0 and certainty is 1. Only the top probability counts, so ( 0.6 , 0.3 , 0.1 ) (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) ( 0.6 , 0.3 , 0.1 ) and ( 0.6 , 0.2 , 0.2 ) (0.6, 0.2, 0.2) ( 0.6 , 0.2 , 0.2 ) both have confidence 0.4. def choice_confidence ( probabilities : list[ float ]) -> float : n = len (probabilities) return ( max (probabilities) - 1 / n) / ( 1 - 1 / n) choice_confidence( list (answer.probabilities.values())) The explorer at the top of this page uses this formula with three options.
